e-8563.knowledge_point: Identifying Connections Between Matrices of a Linear Transformation Relative to Different Bases
e-8563.problem:
Let $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ and $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}}$ be the matrices of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C},$ respectively. If $P_{\small \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{B}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from basis $\mathcal{C}$ to basis $\mathcal{B},$ which of the following statements are true?

- $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{B}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}}\cdot P_{\small \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{B}}^{-1}$

- $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{B}}^{-1} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{B}}$

- $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{B}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small \mathcal{B} \to \mathcal{C}}$
e-8563.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/2e82c232614bec8a98f079ea56d7913ee13e7b457e33e418198278d2e369fc5c.png)

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{B}}^{-1} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{B}},
$$

where $P_{\small \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{B}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$

Solving this equation for $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{B}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}} \cdot P_{\small \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{B}}^{-1}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

e-5516.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Basis Using a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
e-5516.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/48ba234a07831383642525bf18fedcf6ea801576d80702e737d37334a04740e3.png)

Consider the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ with respect to the basis $\mathcal{B}$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small \mathcal{B} \to \mathcal{C}}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$
e-5516.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}\,,
$$

where $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$

Our goal is to compute $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}}.$ First, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-0\cdot (-1)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -7 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -10 \\ 5 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

e-5517.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to the Standard Basis
e-5517.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/fe3c67c0218808ba7b398d1659530d61a4c8ce3eafd196341ba6645ac7076f43.png)

Consider the basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}.$
e-5517.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}$ and standard basis $\mathcal{S}$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{S}} = P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{S}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{S}}}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/d050ac7d04af79ad9b5e7f096e3d21c9808af4a756f43d46ca29beca00dedcc9.png)

First, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{S}}} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & -7 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 3-(-7)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -7 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 13 \\ 3 & -9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

e-5897.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Given Basis
e-5897.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/76bfd9209f632ac8576051154d7e4250d8c4c53ffe843238b6d25835704ce398.png)

Consider the bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2,$ and the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ with respect to the basis $\mathcal{B}$, shown above. Find the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$
e-5897.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}}^{-1},
$$

where $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/cb0c35da5a4bd26c92343d7262efcb7ba7f197cdeea95c2d541b7441a6485804.png)

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/6759e7c098d5375894d540050e3c3dd9e3bb453b0cac7338b9b6754bb635f717.png)

Now, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-0\cdot (-1)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -9 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
$$
[T]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{C}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $C$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $B.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/2e82c232614bec8a98f079ea56d7913ee13e7b457e33e418198278d2e369fc5c.png)

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{C\to B}^{-1}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}.
$$

where ${P}_{C\to B}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{B}.$ Solving this equation for $[T]_{B},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$
[T]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}\cdot [T]_{C}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}^{-1}.
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 5-1\cdot 6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 6 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}\cdot [T]_{C}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 6 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 6 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & 34 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

[T]C=[12−1−3],PC→B=[5611]

Consider the matrix [T]C of a linear transformation T with respect to the basis C and the change-of-coordinates matrix PC→B shown above. Find the matrix of T relative to the basis B.

a
 [23−263−4]
b
 [−716−2−1]
c
[−9−16−1−4]
d
[−7−26−1−5]
e
[−734−15]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation T relative to the bases B and C is given by the following diagram:

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

[T]C=PC→B−1⋅[T]B⋅PC→B.

where PC→B is the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B.

Our goal is to compute [T]B. Solving this equation for [T]B, we obtain the alternative formulation

[T]B=PC→B⋅[T]C⋅PC→B−1.

First, we compute the inverse of PC→B:

PC→B−1=[5611]−1=11⋅5−1⋅6[1−6−15]=[−161−5]

Now, we can compute the matrix of T relative to the basis B:

[T]B=PC→B⋅[T]C⋅PC→B−1=[5611][12−1−3][−161−5]=[−1−80−1][−161−5]=[−734−15]

content.problem:
$$
[T]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{C}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $C$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $B.$
content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/2e82c232614bec8a98f079ea56d7913ee13e7b457e33e418198278d2e369fc5c.png)

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{C\to B}^{-1}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}.
$$

where ${P}_{C\to B}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{B}.$ Solving this equation for $[T]_{B},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$
[T]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}\cdot [T]_{C}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}^{-1}.
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 5-1\cdot 6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 6 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}\cdot [T]_{C}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 6 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 6 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & 34 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
$$
[T]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{C}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $C$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $B.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/2e82c232614bec8a98f079ea56d7913ee13e7b457e33e418198278d2e369fc5c.png)

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{C\to B}^{-1}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}.
$$

where ${P}_{C\to B}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{B}.$ Solving this equation for $[T]_{B},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$
[T]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}\cdot [T]_{C}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}^{-1}.
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 3-2\cdot 4}[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}\cdot [T]_{C}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 8 \\ -8 & 11\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation T relative to the bases B and C is given by the following diagram:

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

[T]C=PC→B−1⋅[T]B⋅PC→B.

where PC→B is the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B.

Our goal is to compute [T]B. Solving this equation for [T]B, we obtain the alternative formulation

[T]B=PC→B⋅[T]C⋅PC→B−1.

First, we compute the inverse of PC→B:

PC→B−1=[3423]−1=13⋅3−2⋅4[3−4−23]=[3−4−23]

Now, we can compute the matrix of T relative to the basis C:

[T]B=PC→B⋅[T]C⋅PC→B−1=[3423][2−4−23][3−4−23]=[−20−21][3−4−23]=[−68−811]

verification.explanation: Recomputing [T]_B=P[T]_C P^{-1}, we have P^{-1}=[[3,-4],[-2,3]] and P[T]_C=[[-2,0],[-2,1]]. Their product is [[-6,8],[-8,11]], agreeing with the revealed solution.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Basis Using a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
$$
[T]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{C}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $C$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $B.$
content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/2e82c232614bec8a98f079ea56d7913ee13e7b457e33e418198278d2e369fc5c.png)

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{C\to B}^{-1}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}.
$$

where ${P}_{C\to B}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{B}.$ Solving this equation for $[T]_{B},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$
[T]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}\cdot [T]_{C}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}^{-1}.
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 3-2\cdot 4}[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}\cdot [T]_{C}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 8 \\ -8 & 11\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
$$
[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1}\,,
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{C}.$ First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)\cdot (-1)-2\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
$$
[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1}\,,
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{C}.$ First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)\cdot (-1)-2\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Basis Using a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
$$
[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1}\,,
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{C}.$ First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 3-1\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 \\ 3 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}20 & -36 \\ 14 & -25\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
$$
[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1}\,,
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{C}.$ First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-4\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 6 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ 18 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

[T]B=[1−121],PB→C=[1041]

Consider the matrix [T]B of a linear transformation T with respect to the basis B and the change-of-coordinates matrix PB→C shown above. Find the matrix of T relative to the basis C.

a
[−3−1185]
b
[1−1−25]
c
[−3−161]
d
[1−16−3]
e
[5−118−3]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation T relative to the bases B and C is given by the following diagram:

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

[T]C=PB→C⋅[T]B⋅PB→C−1,

where PB→C is the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

Our goal is to compute [T]C. First, we compute the inverse of PB→C:

PB→C−1=[1041]−1=11⋅1−4⋅0[10−41]=[10−41]

Now, we can compute the matrix of T relative to the basis C:

[T]C=PB→C⋅[T]B⋅PB→C−1=[1041][1−121][10−41]=[1−16−3][10−41]=[5−118−3]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Basis Using a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
$$
[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1}\,,
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{C}.$ First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-4\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 6 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ 18 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the basis $B$ and standard basis $S$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 3-5\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the basis $B$ and standard basis $S$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 3-5\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 3-5\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Place the basis vectors in the columns of P=[[3,2],[2,1]]. Then [T]_S=P[T]_B P^{-1}, with P^{-1}=[[-1,2],[2,-3]]. Since P[T]_B=[[-7,-8],[-4,-5]], multiplying gives [T]_S=[[-9,10],[-6,7]].

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the basis $B$ and standard basis $S$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 1-2\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -8 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 10 \\ -6 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

B={[32],[21]},[T]B=[−1−2−2−1]

Consider the basis B of R2 and the matrix [T]B of a linear transformation T with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of T relative to the standard basis S.

b
[10−967]

[−910−67]

[67−910]
e

EXPLANATION

The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation T relative to the basis B and standard basis S is given by the following diagram:

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

[T]S=PB→S⋅[T]B⋅PB→S−1,

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is

PB→S=[3221].

First, we compute the inverse of PB→S:

PB→S−1=[3221]−1=13⋅1−2⋅2[1−2−23]=[−122−3].

Now, we can compute the matrix of T relative to the standard basis S:

[T]S=PB→S⋅[T]B⋅PB→S−1=[3221][−1−2−2−1][−122−3]=[−7−8−4−5][−122−3]=[−910−67]

verification.explanation: Rechecking [T]_S=P[T]_B P^{-1}, the basis matrix is P=[[3,2],[2,1]] with inverse [[-1,2],[2,-3]]. The product [[-7,-8],[-4,-5]][[-1,2],[2,-3]] equals [[-9,10],[-6,7]], confirming the revealed solution.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to the Standard Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S.$
content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the basis $B$ and standard basis $S$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 1-2\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -8 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 10 \\ -6 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the basis $B$ and standard basis $S$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-2)\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -23 & 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13

B={[25],[−1−2]},[T]B=[2336]

Consider the basis B of R2 and the matrix [T]B of a linear transformation T with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of T relative to the standard basis S.

a
[−21−2310]
b
[−10−4−3]
c
[1043]
d
[2−123−10]
e
[−2−123−10]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation T relative to the basis B and standard basis S is given by the following diagram:

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

[T]S=PB→S⋅[T]B⋅PB→S−1,

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is

PB→S=[2−15−2].

First, we compute the inverse of PB→S:

PB→S−1=[2−15−2]−1=1(−2)⋅2−(−1)⋅5[−21−52]=[−21−52].

Now, we can compute the matrix of T relative to the standard basis S:

[T]S=PB→S⋅[T]B⋅PB→S−1=[2−15−2][2336][−21−52]=[1043][−21−52]=[−21−2310]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to the Standard Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S.$
content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the basis $B$ and standard basis $S$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-2)\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -23 & 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the basis $B$ and standard basis $S$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -5 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -5 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-4)\cdot 4-3\cdot (-5)}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -3 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -5 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -5 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -5 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -5 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}11 & 8 \\ -10 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the basis $B$ and standard basis $S$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot (-3)-(-1)\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the basis B of R2 and the matrix [T]B of a linear transformation T with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of T relative to the standard basis S.

b
[2−4−13]

Submit

EXPLANATION

The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation T relative to the basis B and standard basis S is given by the following diagram:

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

[T]S=PB→S⋅[T]B⋅PB→S−1,

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is

PB→S=[−32−11].

First, we compute the inverse of PB→S:

PB→S−1=[−32−11]−1=11⋅(−3)−(−1)⋅2[1−21−3]=[−12−13].

Now, we can compute the matrix of T relative to the standard basis S:

[T]S=PB→S⋅[T]B⋅PB→S−1=[−32−11][2223][−12−13]=[−2001][−12−13]=[2−4−13]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to the Standard Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S.$
content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the basis $B$ and standard basis $S$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot (-3)-(-1)\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 16
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 & 4 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 5-3\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -6 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

B={[−14],[−13]},C={[1−1],[−23]},[T]B=[−1−346]

Consider the bases B and C of R2, and the matrix [T]B of a linear transformation T with respect to the basis B, shown above. Find the matrix of T relative to the basis C.

a
[5−610]
b
[7−12−1018]
c
[7353]
d
[4232]
e
[2−3−35]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation T relative to the bases B and C is given by the following diagram:

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

[T]C=PB→C⋅[T]B⋅PB→C−1,

where PB→C is the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

First, let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from B relative to the basis C.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of b1 and b2 relative to the basis C. To do this, we consider the matrix

M=[||||c1c2b1b2||||].

We reduce M using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

M=[1−2−1−1−1343]R2:=R2+R1∼[1−2−1−10132]R1:=R1+2R2∼[10530132]

Hence, PB→C=[5332].

Now, we compute the inverse of PB→C:

PB→C−1=[5332]−1=12⋅5−3⋅3[2−3−35]=[2−3−35]

Finally, we can compute the matrix of T relative to the basis C:

[T]C=PB→C⋅[T]B⋅PB→C−1=[5332][−1−346][2−3−35]=[7353][2−3−35]=[5−610]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Given Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 & 4 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 5-3\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -6 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 17
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & 8 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 8 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -11 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-11 & 3 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-11 & 3 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)\cdot (-11)-4\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -4 & -11\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 11\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-11 & 3 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 11\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}20 & -6 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 11\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Given Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & 8 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 8 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -11 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-11 & 3 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-11 & 3 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)\cdot (-11)-4\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -4 & -11\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 11\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-11 & 3 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 11\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}20 & -6 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 11\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 6\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -4\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 10 & -7 \\ 2 & 0 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 10 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -14 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 10 & -7 \\ 0 & 1 & -7 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -7 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -7 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -7 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 3-(-7)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 7 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 7 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -7 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 7 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & 7 \\ 21 & -15\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 7 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 5 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the bases B and C of R2, and the matrix [T]B of a linear transformation T with respect to the basis B, shown above. Find the matrix of T relative to the basis C.

EXPLANATION

The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation T relative to the bases B and C is given by the following diagram:

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

[T]C=PB→C⋅[T]B⋅PB→C−1,

where PB→C is the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

First, let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from B relative to the basis C.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of b1 and b2 relative to the basis C. To do this, we consider the matrix

M=[||||c1c2b1b2||||].

We reduce M using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

M=[1−110−7206−4]R2:=R2+(−2)R1∼[1−110−702−1410]R2:=12R2∼[1−110−701−75]R1:=R1+R2∼[103−201−75]

Hence, PB→C=[3−2−75].

Now, we compute the inverse of PB→C:

PB→C−1=[3−2−75]−1=15⋅3−(−7)⋅(−2)[5273]=[5273]

Finally, we can compute the matrix of T relative to the basis C:

[T]C=PB→C⋅[T]B⋅PB→C−1=[3−2−75][2574][5273]=[−8721−15][5273]=[950−3]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Given Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 6\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -4\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 10 & -7 \\ 2 & 0 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 10 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -14 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 10 & -7 \\ 0 & 1 & -7 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -7 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -7 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -7 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 3-(-7)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 7 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 7 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -7 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 7 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & 7 \\ 21 & -15\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 7 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 5 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The change-of-coordinates matrix is P=C^{-1}B=[[4,-3],[3,-2]], with P^{-1}=[[-2,3],[-3,4]]. Since P[T]_B=I, we obtain [T]_C=P[T]_B P^{-1}=P^{-1}=[[-2,3],[-3,4]].

after.name: Question 19
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot (-2)-(-3)\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the bases B and C of R2, and the matrix [T]B of a linear transformation T with respect to the basis B, shown above. Find the matrix of T relative to the basis C.

a

EXPLANATION

The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation T relative to the bases B and C is given by the following diagram:

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

[T]C=PB→C⋅[T]B⋅PB→C−1,

where PB→C is the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

First, let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from B relative to the basis C.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of b1 and b2 relative to the basis C. To do this, we consider the matrix

M=[||||c1c2b1b2||||].

We reduce M using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

M=[1−2−212−3−10]R2:=R2+(−2)R1∼[1−2−21013−2]R1:=R1+2R2∼[104−3013−2]

Hence, PB→C=[4−33−2].

Now, we compute the inverse of PB→C:

PB→C−1=[4−33−2]−1=14⋅(−2)−(−3)⋅3[−23−34]=[−23−34]

Finally, we can compute the matrix of T relative to the basis C:

[T]C=PB→C⋅[T]B⋅PB→C−1=[4−33−2][−23−34][−23−34]=[1001][−23−34]=[−23−34]

verification.explanation: Rechecking gives P=C^{-1}B=[[4,-3],[3,-2]] and P^{-1}=[[-2,3],[-3,4]]. Since P[T]_B=I, [T]_C=P[T]_B P^{-1}=[[-2,3],[-3,4]], agreeing with the revealed solution.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Given Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot (-2)-(-3)\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
