after.name: Question 20
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -11\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
after.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 7 & 2 \\ -2 & -1 & -11 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 1-1\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}11 & -13 \\ 6 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the bases B and C of R2, and the matrix [T]B of a linear transformation T with respect to the basis B, shown above. Find the matrix of T relative to the basis C.

EXPLANATION

The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation T relative to the bases B and C is given by the following diagram:

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

[T]C=PB→C⋅[T]B⋅PB→C−1,

where PB→C is the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

First, let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from B relative to the basis C.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of b1 and b2 relative to the basis C. To do this, we consider the matrix

M=[||||c1c2b1b2||||].

We reduce M using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

M=[1172−2−1−11−3]R2:=R2+2R1∼[11720131]R1:=R1−R2∼[10410131]

Hence, PB→C=[4131].

Now, we compute the inverse of PB→C:

PB→C−1=[4131]−1=14⋅1−1⋅3[1−1−34]=[1−1−34]

Finally, we can compute the matrix of T relative to the basis C:

[T]C=PB→C⋅[T]B⋅PB→C−1=[4131][2−1−32][1−1−34]=[5−23−1][1−1−34]=[11−136−7]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Given Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -11\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
content.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 7 & 2 \\ -2 & -1 & -11 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 1-1\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}11 & -13 \\ 6 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
